idiom_name: private collection field + read-only read path (view, copy or iterator) + add/remove operations
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the container in a private field; publish a read path (a read-only view that cannot be mutated through, a defensive copy, or an iterator); publish addX/removeX methods that accept single elements, validate them and update derived state. Remove any setter that installs a whole collection - if bulk replacement is genuinely needed, rename it (replaceAll) so its destructive nature is visible. Choose the read path deliberately: a view is cheap but live and reports violations only at call time, a copy is isolated but costs one allocation and stays shallow, an iterator avoids both but withholds size/contains/random access. Initialize the field to an empty collection in the constructor so no caller has to null-check it.
code_sketch:
owner._items                       # private field, never published
read()  -> view | copy | iterator   # caller may look, not change membership
add(x) / remove(x)                 # only paths that may change membership
# client:
for x in owner.read(): ...          # read through the published path
owner.add(x)                        # never owner._items.push(x)
pitfalls: A getter that returns the live container is the half-refactoring that keeps the original bug: the field is private but membership is still public.
A setter taking a whole collection bypasses every validation and bookkeeping rule; bulk replacement must be an explicit owner operation.
Views and copies are shallow: membership is protected, elements are not - document which one callers get and what it guarantees.

Wrong move: returning Collections.unmodifiableList(field) and calling the result immutable -> the wrapper is a live view, so later owner mutations surface under the caller and shared reads race -> instead return a List.copyOf snapshot, or document the live-view contract and guarantee the owner will not mutate after publication.

Wrong move: paying a defensive copy on every read of a large hot-path collection -> the O(n) allocation per getter call dominates cost and the copy is still shallow, so element mutation leaks anyway -> instead hand out a borrowed read-only view (&[T], std::span, ReadOnlySpan) or move the behaviour the caller wants into the owner so no collection is published at all.

Wrong move: sealing the collection read-only while leaving callers no adequate mutation path -> they route around the owner via reflection, ORM field access or a reintroduced bulk setter -> instead publish explicit add/remove (and replaceAll when bulk is real) so the sanctioned path is easier than the escape hatch.
